lesson.title: Learn Pandas in Python
lesson.goal: load a CSV with pandas, then select, filter, clean and group the data

steps.title: Install pandas and get starter data
steps.instructions: Create a new project folder, download orders.csv from https://github.com/techwithtim/PanadasTutorial into it, and install pandas in the editor terminal with pip install pandas (or uv add pandas).

targets.caption: Install pandas in the project terminal

explanations.topic: Using pip vs pip3 or uv virtual environments

hints: Have you created a project folder containing orders.csv first?
Run pip install pandas (or pip3 install pandas on macOS/Linux) in your integrated terminal.
Alternatively, run uv init . followed by uv add pandas to install it into a .venv environment.
common_mistakes: Using pip instead of pip3 on macOS or Linux
Forgetting to activate or run inside the uv virtual environment after uv add pandas

steps.title: Load and print CSV in main.py
steps.instructions: Create main.py that imports pandas as pd, loads orders.csv with pd.read_csv and prints the DataFrame. Run it in the terminal and check the table output.

targets.caption: Load the CSV file into a DataFrame

hints: How do you import pandas under its standard alias?
Use pd.read_csv("orders.csv") and assign it to df, then call print(df).
Run python main.py or uv run .\main.py in the terminal from the folder containing orders.csv.
common_mistakes: Running the script from a parent directory where orders.csv is not found
Misspelling read_csv or forgetting quotes around "orders.csv"
steps.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv")
print(df)

steps.title: Create notebook and load CSV
steps.instructions: Create and save notebook.ipynb via the Command Palette (Python extension installed). In two cells, load orders.csv into df and run print(df).

targets.caption: Load orders.csv in the first notebook cell

explanations.topic: Why Jupyter Notebooks are useful for data analysis
Installing the VS Code Python extension

hints: Press Ctrl+Shift+P (or Cmd+Shift+P) and search for New Jupyter Notebook.
Select your Python interpreter kernel before executing the first cell.
Put import pandas as pd and df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv") in cell 1, then print(df) in cell 2.
common_mistakes: Running a cell without selecting a Python kernel that has pandas installed
Forgetting to execute cell 1 before running cell 2 that references df
steps.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv")
print(df)

steps.title: Explore DataFrame structure and statistics
steps.instructions: In a new cell of notebook.ipynb, inspect your DataFrame with df.head(), df.tail(), df.info(), df.describe(), df.columns and df.index. Run each and read the output.

targets.caption: Check column data types and entry counts

explanations.topic: df.info() data types and non-null counts

hints: Which methods show the first and last five rows?
Call df.info() and df.describe() with parentheses, and access df.columns and df.index without parentheses.
Run each expression in a cell to view the output.
common_mistakes: Calling df.columns() or df.index() with parentheses instead of accessing them as attributes
Forgetting parentheses on df.head(), df.tail(), df.info(), or df.describe()
steps.code:
df.head()
df.tail()
df.info()
df.describe()
df.columns
df.index

steps.title: Index rows and columns
steps.instructions: In notebook.ipynb, select one column with df["Country"] and several with df[["Country", "Product"]]. Then access a row with df.iloc[10] and a field with df.iloc[10]["Shipped"], running each cell.

targets.caption: Select a single row by position using iloc

explanations.topic: Column indexing returning a Series vs DataFrame

hints: How do you pass a list of column names to df[...]?
Use double square brackets df[["Country", "Product"]] for multiple columns.
Use df.iloc[10] for the row at index 10, and chain ["Shipped"] to get a single value.
common_mistakes: Using single brackets df["Country", "Product"] instead of double brackets df[["Country", "Product"]]
Calling df.iloc(10) with parentheses instead of square brackets

steps.title: Filter rows with boolean conditions
steps.instructions: In notebook.ipynb, filter df with ==, & and |, a numeric comparison, .str.startswith/.str.endswith, and ~ with .isin(). Run each cell (Shift+Enter) to see the filtered tables.

targets.caption: Filter string columns using .str accessor methods

hints: Wrap each condition in parentheses when combining them with & or |.
Use .str before startswith("A") or endswith("a") on a text column.
Use ~ before the condition inside df[...] to invert an .isin([...]) filter.
common_mistakes: Using Python's and/or keywords instead of & and | between Series conditions
Forgetting parentheses around each condition when using & or |

steps.title: Update DataFrame values with loc
steps.instructions: In notebook.ipynb, use df.loc[...] to update rows matching a condition (e.g. change USA to United States in Country), then uppercase the Country column with .str.upper(). Run the cell and display df to see the updated values.

targets.caption: Update matching rows in place using df.loc

explanations.topic: How df.loc selects rows by label or condition

hints: Pass the row condition and target column name separated by a comma inside df.loc[condition, column].
Assign the new value directly with =.
Reassign df["Country"] = df["Country"].str.upper() to update all rows in the column.
common_mistakes: Using df[condition]["Country"] = ... which triggers SettingWithCopyWarning and may not mutate df
Forgetting to assign df["Country"] = ... after calling .str.upper()
steps.code:
df.loc[df["CustomerName"] == "Anna Ivanova", "Product"] = "Tim"
df.loc[df["Country"] == "USA", "Country"] = "United States"
df["Country"] = df["Country"].str.upper()

steps.title: Delete, clean, and rename data
steps.instructions: In notebook.ipynb, drop a row with df.drop(...), handle nulls with df.dropna() or df.fillna(...), and rename a column with df.rename(columns=...). Run the cell and display df to see the result.

targets.caption: Rename a column in place using df.rename

explanations.topic: How inplace=True modifies the DataFrame directly

hints: Remember to assign df = df.drop(39) or pass inplace=True so the deletion persists.
Use df.fillna({"OrderID": 0}, inplace=True) to fill missing values in a specific column.
Pass a dictionary of old-to-new names to the columns parameter in df.rename().
common_mistakes: Calling df.drop(39) without reassigning df or passing inplace=True
Forgetting inplace=True on df.rename() and wondering why the column name did not change
steps.code:
df = df.drop(39)
df.dropna()
df.fillna({"OrderID": 0}, inplace=True)
df.rename(columns={"OrderID": "Order ID"}, inplace=True)

steps.title: Analyze data and export CSV
steps.instructions: In notebook.ipynb, count values with .value_counts(), sum a numeric column per group with .groupby(), sort with .sort_values(), and save with df.to_csv("new_file.csv", index=False). Run each cell to see the counts and grouped sums.

targets.caption: Group by a column and sum values
Save the modified DataFrame to a new CSV file

explanations.topic: Grouping and aggregating values with groupby
Controlling row index export with index=False

hints: Call .value_counts() on df["Country"] to count occurrences of each country.
Chain ["Price"].sum() after df.groupby("Country").
Pass ascending=False to sort_values and index=False to to_csv("new_file.csv", index=False).
common_mistakes: Forgetting index=False in to_csv, which writes an extra unnamed index column to the CSV
Using ascending=True when descending order is intended
steps.code:
df["Country"].value_counts()
df.groupby("Country")["Price"].sum()
df.sort_values("Price", ascending=False)
df.to_csv("new_file.csv", index=False)
